citeinfo.title: Critical mineral deposits of the United States (ver. 3.0, 2026)

descript.abstract: A goal of the USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) program, which partners the USGS with State Geological Surveys, Federal agencies, and the private sector, is to collect new geological, geophysical, geochemical, and topographic (lidar) data in key areas of the U.S., with the purpose of stimulating domestic mineral exploration and production of critical minerals. As a first step, the Earth MRI program identified regional geographic areas within the United States that may have potential to host deposits containing critical minerals. These are the focus areas described in Dicken and others (2022) (https://doi.org/10.5066/P9DIZ9N8). As a further step to meet Earth MRI priorities, mineral deposit information was gleaned from the USGS Mineral Resource Data System (MRDS), the Alaska Resource Data File (ARDF) and USMIN databases, as well as from industry reports and the literature, resulting in a database of 1,271 individual mineral deposits documented to contain critical minerals. In the database, deposits are classified by mineral systems, deposit types, and identified critical minerals. Production and/or resource/reserve numbers confirming the presence of critical minerals are included to further characterize the size, status, and potential of each entry. Deposits are also given a ranked value (1 to 5) determined from their critical mineral status as past, current or future producers, and the presence or absence of known reserves or resources. Out of 1,271 deposits, 412 of the entries are not classified as past or current producers, but have recognized, documented resources. This subset is of particular interest as it represents possible untapped critical mineral potential. Version 3 includes data and updates to version 2 as well as additional mineral deposits for all of the critical minerals included on the 2025 USGS Critical Mineral list (Nassar and others, 2025). The 2025 list added boron, copper, lead, metallurgical coal, phosphate, potash, rhenium, silicon, silver, and uranium to the previous list and removed arsenic and tellurium. We retained arsenic and tellurium for completeness and did not address metallurgical coal in this compilation. References are provided to support production and resource figures.
descript.purpose: The purpose of the geospatial data layers and accompanying data tables is to document the locations, production history, and reported resources of critical minerals contained in U.S. Geological Survey mineral occurrence databases, including the Mineral Resource Data System (MRDS), the USMIN Mineral Deposit Database, and the Alaska Resource Data File (ARDF).

procstep.procdesc:
The following processing step is for the original version of this data release from July 31, 2023. Users should review all processing steps for updates and revisions.
USGS mineral occurrence databases MRDS, ARDF, and USMIN were queried for sites that produced critical minerals in the past or have resources for critical minerals reported by searching for sites that mention a critical mineral commodity. USGS Mineral Commodity Summary reports were examined for mention of active mines for critical mineral commodities. Critical minerals are those included on the 2022 U.S. critical minerals list. Data were also extracted from a compilation of critical mineral focus areas (Dicken and others, 2022). In addition, mining company reports for properties in the United States were compiled along with information reported on company websites and in press releases. Site names, locations, and production and resource data were extracted from the source materials. The sites were plotted in a GIS environment using the focus area boundaries. Focus area names, mineral systems, and deposit types were related to each site. Duplicates were deleted along with any site that did not have either past production data reported or resource information reported. The most recent and reliable data were selected, such as data from technical reports that meet international reporting standards for resources and reserves. Sites that mention past but unquantified production were not included. Production and resource data are reported as noted in source documents (short tons, metric tons, pounds, and so forth). Sites in the final list are called deposits.
2022 critical minerals list - https://www.usgs.gov/news/national-news-release/us-geological-survey-releases-2022-list-critical-minerals.
Full references for sources used can also be found in the associated stand-alone table under the tab called References.
